newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algeria's legal Islamists urge fair elections.
newsitem.headline: Algeria's legal Islamists urge fair elections.

text.p: The leaders of Algeria's two legal Islamist parties said on Thursday a June 5 general election could mark the first step towards ending the North African state's five-year-old civil strife.

But the Islamist leaders, in separate interviews with Reuters, warned that if the polls for the 380-seat National Assembly were not free and fair they could spark a deterioration in the conflict that has claimed 60,000 lives so far.

"If the elections were free and fair and the government respected the outcome then the parliamentary poll will help a great deal in preparing the conditions to resolve the crisis," said Abdallah Djaballah, leader of Nahda Movement.

Mahfoud Nahnah, the leader of Hamas party who won one third of the vote in the 1995 presidential poll, said if the authorities observed a neutral stand during the elections the "poll will be a step in resolving the crisis".

"The political opportunities are not available all the time. We see that the country's political system has an opportunity to establish a democracy through the elections this year," Nahnah said. "We fear Algeria may slid into a deep crisis if this chance to hold a fair election is missed."
Algeria has been without an elected parliament since January 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which the radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) took a huge lead.

About 60,000 people have died in the country's five years of violence locking government forces with Moslem rebels. The FIS was outlawed and it is barred from fielding candidates in the elections. Its leadership abroad have urged a boycott.

"The absence of FIS from the political scene with two Islamist parties competing for the Islamist voters will improve our chances in the elections and it will be the same for some other parties," said Djaballah.
He and Nahnah appeared unenthusiatic about forging alliances with each other or with other groups.
"We call on other parties to coordinate efforts to supervise together the fairness of the elections but the alliances will only be needed inside the elected parliament," said Nahnah.
Hamas is represented in the government with two junior ministers and has seats in the goverment-appointed Transitional National Council (CNT), a quasi-parliament.

"Our participation in the CNT and the government was very positive underscoring our willingness to avoid compounding the crisis. Some people feared that Islamists are violent but our participation showed the Islamists are decent hard workers seeking to serve the people's interests," Nahnah said.
The two men dismissed the National Democratic Rally (RND), created last month by supporters of President Liamine Zeroual as one the front-runners in the parliamentary elections.
"The National Democratic Rally will emerge as a strong party only if it became the spoilt child of the authorities," said Nahnah.
Djaballah said the RND was benefiting the authorities support, including getting headquarters in some provinces without paying money.
"We call on the authorities to be neutral according to the president orders and treat the political parties as equals," said Djaballah.
